Q. 
How were the forecast billing determinants developed? 
4 
A. 
For SC-1 (Residential), SC-2 (Small General), SC-5 (Firm Gas Sales and 
5 
Transportation), SC-7 (Small Volume Firm Gas Sales and Transportation), 
6 
and SC-8 (Gas Sales and Transportation Service with Standby Sales), the 
7 
base delivery revenue forecast was developed based on the forecast 
8 
number of customers and deliveries.  Deliveries were allocated to the 
9 
usage blocks within each service class using ogive analysis.  Ogive 
10 
analysis uses historic bill frequencies to develop a cumulative percentage 
11 
distribution for usage levels within a service class.  The cumulative 
12 
distribution is then used to allocate the forecast deliveries into the usage 
13 
blocks for each service class, after which the deliveries can be priced at 
14 
the applicable rate for the particular block. 
15 
 
16 
 
For SC-6 (Large Volume Interruptible Transportation), SC-9 (Negotiated 
17 
Transportation Services/Special Contracts), SC-10 (Natural Gas Vehicle), 
18 
SC-12 
(Distributed 
Generation 
Service-Non 
Residential), 
SC-13 
19 
(Distributed Generation), SC-14 (Dual Fuel Electric Generators), and New 
20 
York State Electric and Gas Corporation (“NYSEG”), ogive analysis was 
21

not used because these service classes either have negotiated contract 
1

3

V. 
Embedded Cost of Service Study 
4 
A. 
Purpose of ECOSS and Overview of Methodology 
5 
Q. 
Please describe what an ECOSS is and why it is prepared. 
6 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion a utility’s total revenue 
7 
requirement, including plant and other investments, operating expenses, 
8 
depreciation, and taxes, among the rate classes served by the utility.  The 
9 
ECOSS computes the revenue that would need to be collected from each 
10 
rate class to produce the system average target rate of return on rate base.  
11 
This information provides guidance in revenue allocation, and in the 
12 
development of rates, to recover the utility’s revenue requirement from all 
13 
rate classes. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please summarize the methodology employed for the ECOSS. 
16 
A. 
The Company used the same methodology in preparing the ECOSS as in 
17 
Niagara Mohawk’s last two gas rate cases, the 2017 Gas Rate Case and 
18 
Case 12-G-0202 (“2012 Gas Rate Case”).  The ECOSS was prepared by 
19 
analyzing each element of the Company’s revenue requirement, and 
20 
assigning or allocating it among the rate classes.  The ECOSS was 
21 


--- Page 19 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 16 of 77 
performed using a proprietary model developed by HSG Group.  This 
1 
model uses the traditional three-step process: (1) functionalization; (2) 
2 
classification; and (3) class allocation. 
3 
 In the functionalization step, the Company’s cost elements (which 
4 
include costs and expenses, as well as the rate base components) 
5 
are assigned or allocated among each of the gas functions 
6 
identified in Appendix A to the Commission’s November 9, 2001 
7 
Order in Case 00-M-0504 (the “Unbundling Cost Study Case”). 
8 
 In the classification step, each functionalized cost element is 
9 
separated into one or more of demand, commodity, and customer 
10 
cost components. 
11 
 In the class allocation step, each functionally classified cost 
12 
element is assigned or allocated among one or more of the 
13 
Company’s rate classes. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please describe the functionalization step of the ECOSS. 
16 
A. 
In the functionalization step, cost elements are separated among the 
17 
utility’s basic service functions by determining what physical purpose 
18 
each cost element serves. 
19 
 
20 
Q. 
What are the functions included in the ECOSS? 
21 


--- Page 20 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 17 of 77 
A. 
The functions included in the ECOSS are: 
1 
 Gas Supply and Storage - availability and supply of gas and 
2 
storage to meet seasonal and daily peak demands; 
3 
 Transmission - moves gas from supply and storage sources to 
4 
localized distribution facilities; 
5 
 Distribution - moves gas from the transmission system to 
6 
customers’ premises; includes service lines; 
7 
 Billing - connects customers to the system, meters their usage and 
8 
demand, and bills for the services provided; 
9 
 Collections;  
10 
 Sales Promotion; and 
11 
 Gas Procurement. 
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please describe the classification step of the ECOSS. 
14 
A. 
The Company’s gas distribution system is designed, operated, and 
15 
maintained to meet three primary objectives: 
16 
1. Connect customers to the Company’s distribution system; 
17 
2. Meet the aggregate peak design day capacity requirements of all 
18 
customers entitled to service on the peak day; and 
19 
3. Deliver natural gas commodity to customers, whether they are 
20 
sales or transportation customers. 
21 


--- Page 21 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 18 of 77 
 
Each functionalized cost element is classified as being one or more of 
1 
customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-related, depending on 
2 
which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
3 
 
4 
 
Costs that are incurred to connect a customer to the distribution system 
5 
and to operate and maintain those assets, to meter the customer’s usage, 
6 
and to maintain customer accounts, are classified as customer-related.  
7 
Customer-related cost elements are primarily a function of the number of 
8 
customers served and are incurred by the Company regardless of whether 
9 
an individual customer uses any gas.  Customer-related components 
10 
include capital and operating costs of the customer component of 
11 
distribution mains, and capital and operating costs of services, meters, and 
12 
house regulators.  They also encompass the costs of metering, billing, 
13 
customer service, and accounting and collection activities.  Customer-
14 
related cost elements are allocated among the classes based primarily on 
15 
number of customers. 
16 
 
17 
 
Cost elements that are associated with plant that is designed, installed, and 
18 
operated to meet peak hourly or daily customer gas requirements, are 
19 
classified as demand, or capacity, related.  Demand-related components 
20 
include transmission mains, the demand component of distribution mains, 
21 


--- Page 22 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 19 of 77 
as well as localized distribution facilities and dedicated facilities that are 
1 
designed to satisfy individual customer maximum demands.  Demand-
2 
related cost elements are allocated among the classes based on their 
3 
contributions to the peak daily demand for which the system is designed. 
4 
 
5 
Cost elements that generally vary with the volume of gas delivered (i.e., 
6 
throughput) to customers are classified as commodity-related. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Do all costs fit neatly into one of the classifications in the ECOSS – 
9

10 
A. 
Most assets and costs fit into one of the three classifications, but some 
11 
were split between demand and customer based on special studies as 
12 
shown in Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-3), Schedule 9, or based on the 
13 
classification of related assets or other related costs.  All assets and costs 
14 
in the Transmission function were classified as demand-related, and all 
15 
assets and costs in the Billing, Collections, and Sales Promotion functions 
16 
were classified as customer-related.  The costs in the Gas Supply and 
17 
Storage that are recovered in the MCG are classified as commodity-related 
18 
(the amount of costs recovered through the MCG was equal to MCG 
19 
revenue), and the balance of Gas Supply and Storage costs are classified 
20 


--- Page 23 ---

Page 20 of 77 
as demand-related.  Gas Procurement costs are classified as demand-
1 
related. 
2

Within the Distribution function, the costs related to services and meters

5

Q. 
Please describe the process for determining how much of the 
8 
investment in distribution mains should be considered customer-
9 
related versus demand-related. 
10 
A. 
Distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the distribution 
11 
system (customer-related), as well as to provide capacity to meet customer 
12 
requirements on the design day (demand-related).  Therefore, the cost of 
13 
mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related.  
14 
The Company performed a minimum system study to determine the 
15 
customer-related portion of mains (Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-3), Schedule 9F).  
16 
Based on the results of the study, the customer component of mains was 
17 
computed to be 46.1 percent and the demand component 53.9 percent.  
18 
The customer component was allocated among the customer classes based 
19 
on the number of customers.  The demand component was allocated 
20 
among the customer classes based on their contribution to design-day 
21 


--- Page 24 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 21 of 77 
demand. 
1 
 
2 
Q. 
Please describe how the minimum-system study was performed. 
3 
A. 
Minimum-system studies are a widely accepted method to classify mains 
4 
between customer- and demand-related costs.  The customer-related 
5 
component is the portion of cost representing the least-cost system the 
6 
Company would install simply to connect customers, without regard to the 
7 
need to meet demand. 
8 
 
9 
The analysis begins by obtaining from plant and accounting records the 
10 
cost of new mains the Company has installed in recent years, along with 
11 
information about diameter, length, and cost.  Then the installed cost per 
12 
foot is computed for each diameter. 
13 
 
14 
The minimum system ratio is computed as the ratio of (X), the current cost 
15 
of replacing the entire mains distribution system with the minimum 
16 
component, which is two-inch plastic, to (Y), the current cost of replacing 
17 
the entire mains distribution system with plastic of the same diameter as-
18 
presently installed. 
19 
 
20 
This produced a minimum system ratio of 46.1 percent, which represents 
21 


--- Page 25 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 22 of 77 
the portion of total mains cost simply to connect customers (i.e., customer-
1 
related costs) without regard to meeting their design-day demands. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Does the minimum system study fulfill the requirements of the Joint 
4 
Proposal in the 2017 Gas Rate Case? 
5 
A. 
Yes.  Under Section 4.12.4 of the Joint Proposal adopted by the 
6 
Commission in the 2017 Gas Rate Case, the Company agreed to maintain 
7 
data necessary to conduct a minimum system study for distribution mains 
8 
and to provide the study in its next rate case.  The study is presented at 
9 
Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-3), Schedule 9F.

Q. 
Please explain the allocation step of the ECOSS. 
12 
A. 
In the allocation phase of the ECOSS, the cost elements that have been 
13 
functionalized and classified are allocated among the service classes.  
14 
There are two types of allocation factors, or allocators, that are used for 
15 
this purpose: external allocators and internal allocators.  External 
16 
allocators are based on special studies derived from data in the Company’s 
17 
accounting and other records.  For example, the number of customers in 
18 
each rate class is an external allocator that was used in the Company’s 
19 
ECOSS to allocate some of the customer-classified costs.  Other examples 
20 


--- Page 26 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 23 of 77 
of external allocators are annual deliveries, design day requirements, and 
1 
historic bad debt experience. 
2 
 
3 
Internal allocators may be based on a combination of external allocators, 
4 
costs that are directly assigned and/or other internal allocators.  For 
5 
example, the allocator for property insurance expense is based on plant 
6 
investment assigned to each service class; therefore, it is necessary to 
7 
compute plant investment by service class before property insurance costs 
8 
can be allocated among the classes.

Q.  
Please summarize the methodology used to develop the Company’s 
11 
revenue allocation shown on Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-4), Schedule 1. 
12 
A. 
The proposed revenue allocation is intended to move the revenue 
13 
produced by each service class closer to its revenue requirement as 
14 
determined in the ECOSS.   In developing the Company’s proposed 
15 
revenue allocation, the Panel considered the costs to provide the type and 
16 
quality of service required by each service class as determined in the 
17 
ECOSS, while mitigating extreme impacts on service classes, a widely-
18 
accepted concept known as “gradualism.” 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 35 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 32 of 77 
A revenue increase, excluding gross revenue tax, of $41.351 million is 
1

2

3 
in MFC and other revenue, an increase in delivery rates of $43.013 million 
4 
is needed (Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-4, Schedule 3, line 26).  The amount to be 
5

6 
Schedule 3, line 25). 
7 
 
8

10

11

12 
increased revenue requirement fairly, while also promoting the goal of 
13 
gradualism.  The Company determined the position of each class with

respect to the average return and the tolerance band to propose increases. 
15 
 
16 
The overall increase needed (proposed delivery revenue plus proposed

MFC, over present delivery revenue and present MFC) is 10.18 percent.

20

analysis for residential customers is shown in Exhibit__(G-RDP-4), 
10 
Schedule 3B.  The Company’s proposed rate design for SC-1 increase the 
11 
ratio of tail block to mid block, as discussed above.  The results of the 
12 
inclining block study show that further increases in slope at this time 
13 
would cause widely varying effects on different usage levels within the 
14 
class.  Therefore, the Company does not believe that the inclining block 
15 
study should be utilized to design rates in this proceeding.

A. 
The MFC is designed to recover certain expenses associated with the 
20 
Company’s role of providing gas procurement functions for: (1) customers 
21 


--- Page 43 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 40 of 77 
who take firm sales service under SC-1 Residential, SC-2 Small General,

and uncollectible expenses.

IX. 
Revenue Decoupling Mechanism  
7 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s current RDM. 
8 
A. 
Under the Company’s current RDM, a revenue-per-customer (“RPC”) 
9 
target is set for delivery service revenues from customers taking service 
10 
under SC-1, 2, and 7, and actual revenues are trued up against the RPC 
11 
targets annually.  The RDM currently contains RPC targets for six groups 
12 
within these three service classifications: SC-1 Residential Non-Heat, SC-
13 
1 Residential Heat, SC-2 Small General Residential, SC-2 Small General 
14 
Commercial, 
SC-2 
Small 
General Industrial, and SC-7 Small 
15 
Transportation.  
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Is the Company proposing to modify its RDM?  
18 
A. 
Yes.  The Company is proposing the following changes: 
19 
 Implement a revenue per class mechanism for SC-1, SC-2, and SC-
20 
7;  and 
21 


--- Page 51 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 48 of 77 
 Expand the RDM to include a revenue per class RDM for SC-5 
1 
and SC-8. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to implement a revenue per class 
4 
RDM for SC-1, SC-2, and SC-7?  
5 
A. 
The Company is proposing to modify the SC-1, SC-2, and SC-7 RDM to 
6 
be calculated on a revenue per class basis because it better supports the 
7 
Commission’s goals of promoting cost-effective energy conservation.  
8 
This change is consistent with KEDNY and KEDLI’s RDM proposal in 
9 
the their currently pending rate case.   
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to expand the RDM to include SC-5 
12 
and SC-8?  
13 
A. 
The Company is proposing to expand the RDM to include SC-5 and SC-8 
14 
because these classes are eligible to participate in energy efficiency 
15 
programs, and the RDM is intended to allow utilities to promote energy 
16 
efficiency to its customers without jeopardizing the recovery of the costs 
17 
incurred to serve customers.  In addition, the shift from “revenue per 
18 
customer” to “revenue per class” decoupling mechanisms for gas utilities 
19 
in New York State allows the Company to expand the RDM to customer 
20 
classes that were previously not included because of the large diversity in 
21 


--- Page 52 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 49 of 77 
customer load profiles in these classes that made developing an average 
1 
revenue per customer difficult.   
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Has the Company established the revenue per class RDM targets for 
4 
the Rate Year?  
5 
A. 
Yes.  The revenue per class RDM targets are set forth on Exhibit ___ (G-
6 
RDP-7).  
7 
 
8 
Q. 
How will expanding the RDM to SC-5 and SC-8 affect the ETIP 
9 
reconciliation?  
10 
A. 
In the Company’s 2017 Gas Rate Case, ETIP costs were moved into base 
11 
rates and any over/under recoveries were reconciled through the existing 
12 
RDM reconciliations.  For any service classifications that did not have 
13 
RDM, including SC-5 and SC-8, the Company is required to reconcile any 
14 
over/under recoveries of ETIP revenue through a separate reconciliation at 
15 
the end of the current rate plan.   With the expansion of RDM to SC-5 and 
16 
SC-8, the separate ETIP reconciliation will no longer be required for these 
17 
service classes.

17 
Company has updated the calculation of the paperless billing credit as 
18 
shown in Exhibit __ (G-RDP-9), Schedule 1.  The credit is based on 
19 


--- Page 71 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 68 of 77 
Historic Test Year costs adjusted for inflation and represents the 
1

2

3 
Company’s forecast costs for the paperless billing credit decreased to 
4

6 
 
7 
To properly provide credits in the Rate Year to existing electronically 
8 
billed customers (those customers who elected to receive electronic bills 
9 
during the Historic Test Year), an adjustment to the Historic Test Year is 
10 
required to add back the avoided cost of issuing a paper bill to those 
11 
customers so that the revenue requirement assumes all customers receive a 
12

13 
billing credit then passes back an equal and offsetting credit to 
14 
electronically billed customers in the Rate Year.  The Paperless Billing 
15 
Program is intended to be cost and revenue neutral. The net savings 
16 
achieved by the Company (i.e., the cost of envelopes, paper, postage, and 
17 
processing, less the cost to provide an electronic bill), would be returned 
18 
to electronically billed customers in the form of a credit on each bill in the 
19 
Rate Year.  The Historic Test Year paperless billing adjustment was 
20 
removed from the Competitive Billing revenue requirement for the

18 
XII. 
Marginal Cost of Service Study    
19 
Q. 
Please provide an overview of the Gas Marginal Cost Study. 
20 


--- Page 75 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 72 of 77 
A. 
The purpose of the MCS, presented in Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10), is to 
1 
compute the incremental, or marginal, cost to the utility to provide the 
2 
next unit of service, i.e., the next dekatherm of design-day demand or the 
3 
next customer connected.  The results of the MCS are useful as a guide in 
4 
rate design. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
How does an MCS differ from an ECOSS? 
7 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to allocate all the utility’s costs.  MCS 
8 
focuses on the change in costs associated with a change in output.  MCSs 
9 
are forward looking and require estimates of future costs.  In addition, the 
10 
costs included in embedded cost studies may be lumpy because the 
11 
utility’s capacity additions may include more capacity than immediately 
12 
needed, while marginal costs are assumed to be incurred only to meet 
13 
future needs. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Please specify the components of marginal costs in the MCS. 
16 
A. 
The MCS estimates the cost of providing an additional unit of service.  In 
17 
this case, service includes two components: 
18 
 Marginal demand-related costs:  The initial capital cost needed to 
19 
provide an additional unit of gas usage, plus the direct O&M costs 
20 


--- Page 76 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 73 of 77 
related to the assets, and related costs for administrative and 
1 
general (“A&G”), general plant, insurance and property taxes. 
2 
 Marginal customer-related costs:  The initial capital costs needed 
3 
to attach an additional customer to the system, plus the direct 
4 
O&M costs related to the assets, and annual costs for customer-
5 
related activities such as metering, billing and customer support. 
6 
 
7 
In each case, the initial capital costs are converted to an annual cost, 
8 
representing the amount that would be included in the annual revenue 
9 
requirement to reflect return on rate base plus associated income tax, 
10 
depreciation expense, property tax, insurance and related costs for A&G 
11 
activities and general plant.  The annual revenue requirement needed for 
12 
one dollar of initial capital (“Economic Carrying Charge Rate”) for each 
13 
asset type in this MCS (distribution mains, services and meters) is 
14 
presented on Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10) Schedule 8 and Schedule 9. 
15 
 
16 
Q. 
What rate classes were included in the MCS? 
17 
A. 
The MCS used the same rate classes as the ECOSS discussed above. 
18 
 
19 
Q. 
Please describe how the marginal demand-related cost was calculated. 
20 


--- Page 77 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 74 of 77 
A. 
The marginal demand-related cost reflects the Company’s projected 
1 
capital costs for distribution mains to serve new customers, and the 
2 
number of new customers to be served by these mains.  The capacity of 
3 
the new mains was determined by taking the forecast usage per-customer 
4 
in the ECOSS.  This resulted in an initial capital cost per dekatherm, 
5 
which was then inflated from 2016 dollars to 2018 dollars.  Finally, the 
6 
capital cost of transmission mains was added based on the historical ratio 
7 
of transmission mains cost to distribution mains cost, to arrive at a total 
8 
annual demand-related capital cost per annual dekatherm. 
9 
 
10 
The capital cost was converted to an annual revenue requirement 
11 
reflecting return on rate base plus associated income tax, depreciation 
12 
expense, property tax, insurance and related costs for A&G activities and 
13 
general plant, plus direct annual O&M costs for the assets.  The annual 
14 
demand-related cost was computed to be $2.34 per dekatherm delivered, 
15 
which is equivalent to $252.45 per dekatherm of design-day activity.  The 
16 
calculations are presented on Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10), Schedule 2. 
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Please describe how the marginal customer-related cost was 
19 
calculated. 
20 


--- Page 78 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 75 of 77 
A. 
The marginal customer-related cost reflects the Company’s projected 
1 
capital costs for services and meters to serve new customers.  These costs 
2 
are computed in the ECOSS. 
3 
 
4 
The capital costs were converted to annual revenue requirements 
5 
reflecting return on rate base plus associated income tax, depreciation 
6 
expense, property tax, insurance and related costs for administrative and 
7 
general activities and general plant, plus direct annual O&M costs for the 
8 
assets.  In addition, annual costs were added for customer-related activities 
9 
such as metering, billing and customer support.  The calculations are 
10 
presented on Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10), Schedules 4, 5, 6, and 7. 
11 
 
12 
Q. 
Did the Panel calculate a marginal revenue requirement? 
13 
A. 
Yes.  The marginal revenue requirement is the marginal demand-related 
14 
cost times annual usage, plus the marginal customer-related cost times the 
15 
number of customers.  The calculations are presented on Exhibit ___ (G-
16 
RDP-10), Schedule 1. 
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Did the Panel use the results of the MCS to calculate any particular 
19 
rates? 
20 


--- Page 79 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 76 of 77 
A. 
Yes, as shown on Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10), Schedule 10, the MCS was 
1 
used to determine the Excelsior Jobs Program rate.  Schedule 10 identifies 
2 
the unit costs produced in the MCS and multiplies them by design day 
3 
Dekatherms and number of customers in the Rate Year to obtain the total 
4 
marginal cost for the Rate Year.  The total marginal cost is then reduced 
5 
by the minimum usage charges.  The remaining marginal costs are then 
6 
divided by Rate Year therms to obtain a volumetric rate, as shown on 
7 
Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-10), Schedule 10. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Is the Panel proposing to make any modifications to the EJP rates 
10 
supported by the MCS? 
11 
A. 
Yes.  The marginal cost rates calculated in the MCS exceed the otherwise 
12 
applicable standard tariff rates for each service classification.  Therefore, 
13 
we are proposing to phase in the marginal cost increases over six years to 
14 
moderate the bill impacts for these customers and to allow them to 
15 
continue receiving a discount from standard tariff rates.  The Company’s 
16 
proposed phase in provides a marginal rate discount of 50 percent in the 
17 
Rate Year, thereafter discounts would decrease 10 percent each year for 
18 
five years. The Company did not propose a five year phase in 
19 
commencing with Rate Year 4 EJP rates, similar to the Electric Rate 
20 
Design Panel’s proposal, because Rate Year EJP rates would have been 
21 


--- Page 80 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 77 of 77 
higher than standard tariff rates, excluding ETIP, for all service 
1 
classifications.  In addition, an ETIP adder needs to be included in the 
2 
marginal cost rates applicable to EJP customers because they are eligible 
3 
to participate in company sponsored energy efficiency programs and the 
4 
marginal cost rates do not include ETIP costs.  The Company may re-
5 
evaluate the proposed phase-in of the EJP rates depending on the final 
6 
revenue requirement in this case. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Does this conclude the Panel’s testimony? 
9 
A. 
Yes, it does.

Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The testimony of the Rate Design Panel describes the purpose of performing an Embedded Cost 
of Service Study (“ECOSS”), and summarizes the methodology used to prepare the ECOSS in 
this proceeding of Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) (“NiMo-Gas” or the “Company”).  
The testimony describes the three-step ECOSS process (functionalization, classification, class 
allocation) used to analyze each element of the revenue requirement, in order to assign or 
allocate it among the rate classes. 
This Schedule 10 describes the ECOSS methodology in more detail.  Part 1 describes the three-
step ECOSS process. 
Part 2 describes how each element of the revenue requirement (rate base, expense and revenue) 
was assigned or allocated in each of the three steps.  Rate base, expenses and revenues are 
identified using the Uniform System of Accounts (FERC Accounts).  Part 2 serves as a guide 
when reviewing the other schedules in this exhibit. 
Part 1. DETAILED ECOSS METHODOLOGY 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion fairly a utility’s total revenue requirement, including 
plant and other investments, operating expenses, depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes 
served by the utility.  The ECOSS computes for each rate class the revenue to be collected to 
produce the overall required rate of return on rate base.  This information provides valuable 
guidance in revenue allocation, and in the development of rates, to recover the revenue 
requirement from all rate classes. 
The three steps of the ECOSS are: 
Functionalization-  Cost elements are separated among the utility’s basic service 
functions, by determining what physical purpose each cost element serves.  The 
Company’s functions are: Gas Supply and Storage; Transmission; Distribution; Billing; 
Collections; Sales Promotion; and Procurement. 
Classification-  Each functionalized cost element is classified as Customer-related 
(connect customers to the distribution system); Demand-related (meet design day 
capacity requirements) or Commodity-related (deliver gas commodity to customers). 
Class Allocation-  Cost elements that have been functionalized and classified are 
allocated among the service classes, using an appropriate allocation factor for each cost 
element.  Allocation factors can be external (e.g., number of customers, deliveries, design 


--- Page 217 ---
Exhibit___ (G-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 2 of 5 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
day requirements sales and historical bad debt experience) or internal (e.g., property 
insurance is based on plant investment). 
Part 2. ALLOCATOR FOR EACH ELEMENT OF THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT 
A. Rate Base 
1. Intangible Plant (FERC Accounts 301-303) 
Primarily the cost of franchises and other rights.  Allocated in proportion to plant 
investment. 
2. Transmission Plant (FERC Accounts 365-368) 
Transmission plant moves natural gas from suppliers to the distribution system, and is 
sized to meet design day requirements.  Classified as Demand and allocated among the 
rate classes based on design day requirements. 
3. Distribution Plant (FERC Accounts 374-386) 
Mains- Distribution mains connect customers to the distribution system (i.e., customer-
related) and provide capacity to meet design day customer requirements (i.e., demand-
related).  Therefore the cost of mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly 
demand-related.  The customer-related portion is the cost of connecting customers, but 
with no load carrying capacity.  This customer component was computde to be 46.12 
percent of the total cost of mains, based on the minimum system performed by the 
Company.  The customer component was allocated among the classes based on the 
number of customers.  The balance, the demand component, was allocated among the 
classes based on design-day requirements. 
Measuring & Regulating Equipment- Sized for design day operation, therefore 
classified as demand-related and allocated among the rate classes based on design day 
requirements. 
Services- Services connect the customer to the distribution mains.  There is a direct 
correspondence between number of customers and number of services; therefore, 
services are classified as customer-related.  The costs are estimated based on the 
current cost for a typical service line for each rate class, which reflects the design day 
requirements for customers based on their rate classes. 
Meters- Meters (including installation costs and house regulators) are classified as 
customer-related, and allocated based on the current cost for a typical meter for 
customers in each rate class. 


--- Page 218 ---
Exhibit___ (G-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 3 of 5 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Land, Structures and Improvements and Other Distribution Plant- Allocated in 
proportion to all other Distribution Plant accounts. 
4. General Plant (FERC Accounts 389-399) 
Primarily Structures & improvements; Tools, shop & garage; and office furniture and 
equipment.  General plant was functionalized, classified and class allocated in 
proportion to the direct labor content of operating and maintenance expense, because 
these assets primarily support direct labor. 
5. Depreciation Reserve (FERC Accounts 108 and 111) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
6. Other Rate Base Items 
Materials & Supplies (which includes prepayments) and Cash Working Capital (non-
supply) were allocated in proportion to non-gas O&M costs.  Accumulated Deferred 
Income Tax and CWIP were allocated in proportion to plant in service.  Regulatory 
Assets and Earnings Base Adjustment were allocated in proportion to rate base.  
Storage Gas was allocated based on seasonal (winter) requirements.  Cash Working 
Capital (supply) was allocated in proportion to annual gas deliveries. 
B. Expenses 
1. Gas Costs (FERC Accounts 804-813)- Allocated in proportion to GAC revenue 
2. Storage Plant O&M (FERC Accounts 840-849)- Classified as Demand and allocated 
based on seasonal requirements 
3. Transmission O&M (FERC Accounts 850-867)- Allocated in proportion to 
Transmission plant (classified as Demand and allocated based on class design day 
requirements) 
4. Distribution O&M (FERC Accounts 870-894) 
O&M for Mains, Services, Meters, Regulating Equipment- Allocated on the same basis 
as the assets to which they relate. 
Operations Supervision & Engineering and Operations Supervision & Engineering- 
Allocated based on direct labor content of O&M accounts 
Other O&M – Classified based n Labor content; Demand component was allocated and 
based design day requirements and customer component on number of customers. 
 


--- Page 219 ---
Exhibit___ (G-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 4 of 5 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
5. Customer Accounts Expenses (FERC Accounts 901-919) 
These accounts were functionalized among Collections, Billing and Distribution based 
on a study of competitive functions performed by the utility.  The accounts are all 
customer-related. 
Supervision (Account 901)-  Allocated in proportion to Customer records and 
collections (Account 903) 
Meter reading (Account 902)-  Allocated based on the investment in meters 
Customer records and collections (Account 903)-  Billing-related activities are Print 
and mail bills and Billing inquiries.  Collections-related activities are a portion of Call 
center and Credit & collections.  Distribution-related activities are the balance of Call 
center, Credit & collections, Collections and Field Collections. 
Each functionalized activity was allocated among the rate classes using an appropriate 
allocation factor, and the results were summed to compute allocators for Account 903- 
Distribution, Account 903- Billing and Account 903- Collections. 
Uncollectible accounts expense (Account 904)-  Allocated based on historical write-off 
experience. 
Miscellaneous customer accounts (Account 905)-  Activities support customer contact; 
allocated in proportion to Account 903. 
Customer assistance expenses (Account 908)-  )-  Customer assistance programs were 
allocated based on number of customers served.  Discounts offered to low income 
customers, and economic development grants, were allocated based on the Company’s 
overall revenue requirement.  Energy efficiency programs were allocated based on firm 
gas deliveries. 
Demonstration & selling (Account 912) and Advertising (Account 916)-  Allocated 
based on annual delivery volumes. 
6. Administrative & General expenses (FERC Accounts 920-939) are grouped as follows: 
 Most A&G expenses are labor-related, and are functionalized, classified and 
allocated in proportion to direct labor content of O&M accounts 
 Plant-related expenses are functionalized, classified and allocated in proportion 
to according to gross plant 


--- Page 220 ---
Exhibit___ (G-RDP-3) 
Schedule 10 
Page 5 of 5 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation (Gas) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
 Other expenses are Regulatory commission expense (Account 928) which was 
allocated based on Rate base, and Miscellaneous General Expense (Account 
930.2) which was allocated based on Gas delivery volumes 
7. Depreciation and Amortization Expense (FERC Accounts 403-407) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
8. Taxes other than on income 
Property taxes were allocated in proportion to plant, excluding services and meters.  
Payroll taxes were allocated in proportion to direct labor content.  Other taxes were 
allocated in proportion to plant. 
9. Income Tax Expense 
Income Tax Expense at present rates was allocated in proportion to Pretax income at 
present rates.  Income Tax Expense at the revenue requirement (i.e., proposed rates) 
was computed based on the target return used to develop the revenue requirement. 
C. Revenue 
Revenue from base delivery charges, GAC, MFC and SBC was allocated based on 
forecast revenue at present rates. 
Late payment revenue was allocated based on historical write-off experience.  Off-
system sales revenue was allocated based on the overall revenue requirment.  Revenue 
representing recovery of certain costs (supervision of field construction was allocated 
in proportion to the O&M accounts where the costs are reflected.  Revenue from Net 
Revenue Sharing classes (SC 6, SC 9 and SC 14), discounts offered to customers and 
miscellaneous revenue were allocated based on the Company’s overall revenue 
requirement

Schedule 1 
Description of the Tariff Alignment Approach 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


--- Page 350 ---
REPORT PURSUANT TO SECTION 4.12.5 OF 2017 JOINT PROPOSAL TO STREAMLINE 
GENERAL SECTION OF GAS TARIFFS FOR NATIONAL GRID’S NEW YORK 
OPERATING COMPANIES 
 
Section 4.12.5 of the Joint Proposal (“2017 Joint Proposal”) approved by the Public Service 
Commission’s “Order Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal and Establishing Electric and Gas Rate 
Plans” issued and effective March 15, 2018 in Cases 17-G-0239, et al., requires that the Niagara 
Mohawk Power Corporation d/b/a National Grid (“Niagara Mohawk” or “Company”) “conduct a 
study to streamline the general sections of PSC 219 with its downstate affiliates and file a report 
in its next base rate case.”  Accordingly, the Company submits this report summarizing the results 
of its extensive study to identify portions of its gas tariff, PSC 219, that could be aligned with the 
tariff provisions of its downstate affiliates, The Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid 
NY (“KEDNY”) and KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid (“KEDLI”).  The 
Company notes that this report does not propose changes to any of the tariffs at this time – it merely 
identifies areas that the Company believes can be modified to better align the tariffs of the three 
New York operating companies.  Therefore, the Company is not providing any redlined proposed 
tariff revisions. 
 
The results of the Company’s analysis to streamline the general sections of its gas tariff with those 
of KEDNY and KEDLI are shown in Schedules 2 and 3 hereto.  The Company’s effort centered 
around identifying portions that can be (i) modified to mirror language found in the Public Service 
Law or the Commission’s regulations under 16 NYCRR, where applicable or (ii) eliminated as 
outdated or repetitive.  Further, because there are operational differences among the three 
companies, the Company limited its analysis to only those provisions that will not impact the 
operations of any of the companies. 
 
Schedule 2 provides the Company’s analysis of the general sections of the three tariffs other than 
the definitions section.  As shown therein, one way to streamline the general section would be to 
reorganize the sections such that they appear in the same order as suggested under Column A.  
Columns C, D, and E identify where each section currently appears in each tariff.  Column F 
identifies sections that can be further aligned.  For example, the “Service Re-establishment 
Charge” section can be modified such that all the applicable charges appear in one section, rather 
than in several places throughout the tariff (as noted in Column F, the re-establishment charges 
appear in two additional places for Niagara Mohawk”).  Column F also notes where any further 
changes would be inappropriate and/or inapplicable.   
 
Schedule 3 is a list of all the definitions found in the three tariffs, listed in alphabetical order.  The 
Company identified several ways that the definitions section can be streamlined for each of the 
tariffs.  First, the Company identified certain terms that appear in at least one of the tariffs but not 
in others and added such words to the extent appropriate.  For example, the term “Btu” or “British 
Thermal Unit” was added to KEDNY’s tariff based on the definition that appears in KEDNY’s 
Gas Transportation Operating Plan Manual.  Also, the Company identified certain terms that would 
be better organized in clusters.  For example, the terms “Non-Residential Applicant” and 
“Residential Applicant” would be better organized under the term “Applicant” instead of 
appearing in alphabetical order under “N” and “R” respectively.  Further, the Company identified 
that a list of relevant abbreviated terms should appear under the definitions section for each of the 
Exhibit___(G-RDP-13)
Schedule 1
Page 1 of 2


--- Page 351 ---
tariffs.  Finally, the Company identified terms that are used interchangeably and can be presented 
as one definition.  For example, the definition of the term “Marketer” is identical to that of the 
term “Energy Service Company” or “ESCO,” so only one definition is required.   Please note that 
the majority of the identified areas for streamlining do not concern changes to the actual definition 
of the terms, as such changes may result in unintended consequences in the Company’s operations. 
 
In conclusion, the Company’s comprehensive effort identifies areas of the general section of the 
Company’s tariff that can be streamlined/aligned with those of KEDNY and KEDLI.  Based on its 
analysis, the Company concluded that many of the differences in the language of the tariff 
provisions stem from operational differences in each service territory and should remain 
unchanged.  However, the Company identified many areas that can be streamlined, including the 
organizational structure of the general section for the three companies.  The Company submits that 
this report satisfies the requirement under Section 4.12.5 of the 2017 Joint Proposal.

Actual heating degree days. Degree days are calculated by subtracting the average daily 
temperature (sum of the daily high and the daily low divided by two) from 65 degrees F. 
The remainder is the number of degree days for the day. Heating degree days result 
when the remainder is a positive number, (i.e., when the average temperature is below 
65.
N/A
Actual heating degree days. Degree days are calculated by subtracting the average daily 
temperature (sum of the daily high and the daily low divided by two) from 65 degrees F. 
The remainder is the number of degree days for the day. Heating degree days result 
when the remainder is a positive number, (i.e., when the average temperature is below 65 
degree F). The heating degree days are then summed over the days that are in the billing 
cycle.
AHDD
N/A
AHDD, or Actual Heating Degree Days, are the actual difference between 65 degrees and 
the average of the minimum and maximum outdoor dry bulb temperatures for a 
particular day. AHDD are always zero when that average is equal to or above 65 degrees 
F.

revenue taxes, the minimum charge and the cost of gas.

the average cost of gas per unit as used in the Monthly Cost of Gas (MCG) calculation by 
the units of gas
used.

Applicable to Sellers participating in the Company’s Daily Balancing Program. The 
Aggregate Daily Imbalance Percentage is calculated by subtracting: 1) the telemetered 
daily consumption grossed up for UFG of the Seller’s pool from: 2) the quantity of gas 
the Seller delivers to the city gate for the pool and dividing this difference by: 3) the 
telemetered daily consumption grossed up for UFG of the pool.
Applicable to Sellers participating in the Company’s Daily Balancing Program. The

telemetered daily consumption grossed up for LAUF of the pool.

Base and Thermal Methodology
N/A
N/A
"Daily Baseload" equals the customer's average daily usage in the two months of lowest 
daily usage during the period of June through September. Annual Baseload equals Daily 
baseload multiplied by 365. Thermal usage equals total usage during the twelve-month 
period minus Annual Baseload. "Degree Day Usage" equals Thermal Usage divided by 
the total number of degree days during the twelve-month period. The Maximum Peak 
Day Quantity equals the product of Degree Day Usage multiplied by 75 plus Daily 
Baseload
Base Year

December 1, 1999.
The first full year of the operation of the NYISO starting December 1, 1999
N/A

hours of the Base Year.

Customer's Commodity Account
Pursuant to Service Classification Nos. 5 and 7 and 13, the amount of natural gas,

redelivery to the Customer and that the Company is holding such amount of the 
customer's gas in storage. A negative balance in the Customer's Commodity Account 
means that the Customer has used more natural gas than has been delivered to the 
Company for redelivery to the Customer.

Release of Capacity - All capacity allocated to the Monthly Balancing Service customers 
of a single Marketer will be released by Niagara Mohawk to the Marketer on behalf of 
the customer in a prearranged capacity release transaction at maximum demand rates in 
accordance with the capacity release provisions of the tariff of the applicable pipeline. 
The term of each such release will be for one calendar month. All releases will occur in 
each month of the year and will be made subject to recall as further described in Rule 4C. 
DTI, TGP, IGT, Union, and TransCanada capacity is allocated to Monthly Balancing Service 
customers equal to percentages of their Maximum Peak Day Quantity as further defined 
in Leaf 171, provided the customer has a positive thermal response. The percentages are 
indicated in the Niagara Mohawk Gas Transportation Operating Procedure. The 
Company reserves the right to change the capacity and allocation, as needed, to 
maintain the Company’s system reliability.

Daily Cash Out Price
Applicable to Sellers participating in either the Company’s Core or Non-Core Monthly 
Balancing Program or Daily Balancing Program reflected as a dollar per dekatherm price.
a) Core Monthly Balancing Program:
The simple average of the following interstate pipeline gas
prices for the date of flow published in Platt’s Gas Daily Price
Guide, Daily Price Survey:
Transco – Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price
Texas Eastern – Tx. Eastern M3 mid-point price
Iroquois – Iroquois Zone 2 mid-point price.
b) Non-Core Monthly Balancing Program:
The Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price for the date of flow published
in Platt’s Gas Daily Price Guide, Daily Price Survey and is
reflected as a per dekatherm price
c) Daily Balancing Program:
A weighted average dollar per dekatherm price determined for each Seller proportionate 
to the amount of gas that the Seller delivers on each interstate pipeline to the 
Company’s city gate. The interstate pipeline gas prices used to compute the Daily Cash 
Out Price are obtained from Platt’s Gas Daily Price Guide, Daily Price Survey for date of 
flow as follows:
Transco – Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price
Texas Eastern – Tx. Eastern M3 mid-point price
Iroquois – Iroquois Zone 2 mid-point price
Tennessee – Tx, Eastern M3 mid-point price
Applicable to Sellers participating in either the Company’s Core or Non-Core Monthly 
Balancing Program or Daily Balancing Program reflected as a dollar per dekatherm price: 
1. Core Monthly Balancing Program: The simple average of the following interstate 
pipeline gas prices for the date of flow published in Platt’s Gas Daily Price Guide, Daily 
Price Survey: Transco – Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price Texas Eastern – Tx. Eastern M3 
mid-point price Iroquois – Iroquois Zone 2 mid-point price 2. Non-Core Monthly 
Balancing Program: The Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price for the date of flow 
published in Platt’s Gas Daily Price Guide, Daily Price Survey. 3. Daily Balancing 
Program: A weighted average price determined for each Seller proportionate to the 
amount of gas that the Seller delivers on each interstate pipeline to the Company’s city 
gate. The interstate pipeline gas prices used to compute the Daily Cash Out Price are 
obtained from Platt’s Gas Daily Price Guide, Daily Price Survey for date of flow as 
follows: Transco – Transco Zone 6 NY mid-point price Texas Eastern – Tx. Eastern M3 mid-
point price Iroquois – Iroquois Zone 2 mid-point price Tennessee – Tx. Eastern M3 mid-
point price
During the Winter (November -April), the daily cashout rate will include allocations of 
Gas Daily DTI North Point common (mid-point) plus DTI South Point/Mid-Point plus 
Iroquois Receipts plus Tennessee Zone 6 plus the respective DTI, Iroquois Receipts and 
Tennessee FT variable and fixed charges plus losses to the Company’s city gate. During 
the Summer (May – October), the daily cashout rate will include allocations of Gas Daily 
DTI North Point common (mid-point) plus DTI South Point/Mid-Point plus DTI FT variable 
and fixed charges plus losses to the Company’s city gate. When the Gas Daily DTI North 
Point/Mid Point price is not posted, the Gas Daily DTI South Point/Mid Point price will be 
used.

DDF
Average degree day factor in therms/heating degree day, is the estimated number of 
therms/heating degree days required to provide space heating for the average 
customer. DDF is determined separately for each customer classification and will be 
revised annually to reflect the temperature sensitivity reflected in the new throughput 
forecast. DDFs for the weather normalization period will be shown on the Statement of 
Weather Normalization Clause Adjustment.
"DDF", or degree day factor in dekatherms per heating degree day, is the estimated 
number of dekatherms used for space heating for each degree of a degree day, based on 
average usage by customers to which this adjustment applies. DDF is determined 
separately for each customer category and may be revised annually to reflect the 
temperature sensitivity reflected in the prior heating season's sales to customers to 
which the adjustment applies. DDF for the weather normalization period will be shown 
on the Statement of Weather Normalization Adjustment Factors.
Average degree day factor in therms/heating degree day, is the estimated number of 
therms/heating degree day required to provide space heating for the average customer. 
DDF is determined separately for each customer classification and will be revised 
annually to reflect the temperature sensitivity reflected in the new throughput forecast. 
DDFs for the weather normalization period will be shown on the Statement of Weather
Normalization Degree Day Factors and Base Loads.

HDD
N/A
"HDD", or Heating Degree Days, are the difference between 65 degrees Fahrenheit (F) 
and the mean of the extremes of the dry bulb temperature during a day. HDD of a day is 
always zero when the mean temperature is above 65 degrees. A heating degree day is 
each degree of temperature difference. Heating degree days also refer to the cumulative 
heating degree days experienced over a period of time more than one day.

Tier 1 17.5 mmBTU/Mwh for older, simple cycle peaking units (i.e.

1998)
Tier 2 11.0 mmBTU/Mwh for Rankine Cycle steam units
Tier 3 10.0 mmBTU/Mwh for new, simple cycle peaking units
Tier 4 7.4 mmBTU/Mwh for combination cycle plants

section IX.B.5.

Monthly Total Value Added Charge
The Monthly Total Value Added Charge is calculated as follows: The Base Year Spark 
Spread is subtracted from the Spark Spread for each hour of the Test Year. Five percent 
(5%) of this difference is divided by the Customer’s Heat Rate and multiplied by the 
number of dekatherms delivered to the Customer during the same Test Year hour. The 
resulting products are summed for each month of the Test Year. If such monthly value is 
less than or equal to zero, the Monthly Total Value Added Charge for that month will be 
zero. If such monthly value is greater than zero, such monthly value is the Monthly Total 
Value Added Charge for that month.
The Monthly Total Value Added Charge is calculated as follows: The Base Year Spark 
Spread is subtracted from the Spark Spread for each hour of the Test Year. Five percent 
(5%) of this difference is divided by the Customer’s Heat Rate and multiplied by the 
number of dekatherms delivered to the Customer during the same Test Year hour. The 
resulting products are summed for each month of the Test Year. If such monthly value is 
less than or equal to zero, the Monthly Total Value Added Charge for that month will be 
zero. If such monthly value is greater than zero, such monthly value is the Monthly Total 
Value Added Charge for that month.
Five percent of the difference between 1) The Spark Spread for each hour of the month 
the generator actually operated and 2) the applicable Base Year Spark Spread will be 
calculated. The resulting amount is multiplied by the Customers MWH Generated Output 
during the same Test Year hour. The resulting dollars for each hour are summed for each 
month of the Test Year. If such monthly value is less than or equal to zero, the Monthly 
Total Value Added Charge for that month will equal zero. If such Monthly Total Value 
Added Charge is greater than zero, such monthly value is the Monthly Total Value Added 
Charge for that month.

Operational Flow Order
The Company shall have the right to issue Operational Flow Orders (OFOs) in order to 
maintain system integrity or to ensure Company's continued ability to provide service to 
its firm customers. The use and issuance of OFOs are set forth in the Company's Gas 
Transportation Operating Procedures Manual, Section VIII, as filed with the Public Service 
Commission.
The Company shall have the right to issue Operational Flow Orders (OFOs) in order to 
maintain system reliabilty or to ensure Company's continued ability to provide service to 
its firm customers. The use and issuance of OFOs are set forth in the Company’s Gas 
Transportation Operating Procedures Manual, Section VIII, as filed with the Public Service 
Commission.
Forced Balancing Operational Flow Order - During any period in which the Company's 
ability to accommodate imbalances is restricted or impaired, Niagara Mohawk may, upon 
eight hours advance notice, impose a Forced Balancing Operational Flow Order ("Forced 
Balancing OFO"). When a Forced Balancing OFO is imposed for under deliveries, usage by 
customers for whom a Marketer is providing Daily Balancing Service must not exceed 
deliveries by more than 2-50% as specified in the OFO. When a Forced Balancing OFO is 
imposed for over deliveries, a Marketer’s deliveries must not exceed usage by 
customers for whom the marketer is providing Daily Balancing Service by more than 2-
50% as specified in the OFO. Direct Customers are also subject to Forced Balancing OFO 
requirements for under and over deliveries. Marketers/Direct Customers will be assessed 
a penalty equal to the currently effective rate per Dth per day for unauthorized usage in 
accordance with Rule 3.3.1 of this schedule for imbalances that exceed the OFO limit. 
Forced Balancing OFO’s will not be used to simultaneously restrict over deliveries and 
under deliveries.

Added Charge over/under collected. This charge is the difference between the sum of 
the Value Added Charges billed to the Customer in the Calendar Year and the 
Customer’s Actual Value Added Charge in the Calendar Year. The Reconciliation Charge 
may be adjusted to ensure the resulting Value Added charge is in accordance with 
Section F.1.d of this Service Classification.

Customer’s Actual Value Added Charge in the Calendar Year. The Reconciliation Charge 
may be adjusted to ensure the resulting Value Added charge is in accordance with

transaction costs, and gains and losses associated with transactions made in 
commodities exchanges or with other risk management entities.

System Performance Adjustment (SPA) 
Mechanism
To take effect starting January 1, 2018 applicable to sales customers served under SC 1, 2, 
3, 9, 15, 16, and 17 and to transportation customers served under SC 5. The 
determination period for the SPA rate is the 12 months ending each August 31st. The

actual system LAUF is less than the LAUF Target or a surcharge if actual system LAUF 
exceeds the LAUF Target.
To take effect starting January 1, 2015 applicable to sales customers served under SC 1, 2,

SPA rate takes effect each January 1st of the upcoming calendar year and is a credit if 
actual system LAUF is less than the LAUF Target or a surcharge if actual system LAUF 
exceeds the LAUF Target.
A SPA per therm rate will be applicable to the SC Nos. 1, 2, 3, 12 and 13 sales customers 
and the SC Nos. 1MB, 2MB, 5, 7, 8, 12MB, 12DB and 13MB transportation customers. The

Transition Costs
Transition costs are costs incurred by the Company from its interstate pipelines as a 
result of the implementation of Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order No. 
636 and/or from customers transferring to non-core service or firm transportation 
service. These costs include, but are not limited to: unrecovered gas costs remaining 
from the pipeline's termination of sales service (Account 191), new facility costs incurred 
to implement FERC Order No. 636, gas supply realignment (GSR) and stranded facility 
costs, and stranded cost on the utility system from transfers to non-core service or to 
firm transportation service.
Transition Costs incurred by the Company from its pipeline gas suppliers or transporters 
as a result of the implementation of Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Order No. 
636, shall be recovered by the Company as follows:
(a) Unrecovered gas costs remaining when the pipeline terminates sales service shall be 
recovered from Service Classification Nos. 1A, 1AR, 1B, 1BR, 1B-DG, 2, 3, 4A, 4A-CNG, 4B, 
7 and 21 through their applicable Monthly Cost of Gas.
(b) New facility costs incurred to implement FERC Order No. 636 and reflected in pipeline 
base rates shall be recovered from Service Classification Nos. 1A, 1AR, 1B, 1BR, 1B-DG, 2, 
3, 4A, 4A-CNG, 4B, 7,17, 18 and 21 through their applicable Monthly Cost of Gas.
(c) Gas Supply Restructuring (GSR) costs and Stranded Facility costs shall be recovered 
from the Gas Adjustment applicable to Service Classification Nos. 1A, 1AR, 1B, 1BR, 1B-
DG, 2, 3, 4A, 4A-CNG, 4B, 7 and 21, as well as surcharges listed on the Company's 
Statements of Rates and Charges for Service Classification Nos. 17 and 18.

Value Added Charge
A unitized per dekatherm rate, derived from the increase from the Base Year Spark 
Spread to the Test Year Spark Spread, adjusted for prior period Reconciliation Charges. 
The Value Added Charge may be adjusted in accordance with Section F.1.d of this Service 
Classification.
A unitized per dekatherm rate, derived from the increase from the Base Year Spark 
Spread to the Test Year Spark Spread, adjusted for prior period Reconciliation Charges. 
The Value Added Charge may be adjusted in accordance with Section F.1.d of this Service 
Classification.
Is a unitized per therm rate established for each Effective Period which is applied to every 
therm delivered by the Company to the Customer or the Customer’s Annual Minimum 
Bill Obligation whichever is greater. The Value Added Charge reflects the increase in the 
Spark Spread from the Base Year to the Test Year. The Value Added Charge for the 
Effective Period March 15, 2006 through April 30, 2007 equals the Annual Total Value 
Added Charge for the Test Year ending December 31, 2005 divided by the number of 
therms the Company delivered to the Customer during the Test Year. If the Customer 
does not have twelve months of consumption data for the Test Year that Customer will 
be assigned a Value Added Charge equal to the average of all the customers Value 
Added Charge within the applicable heat rate tier level. The Value Added Charge for all 
Effective Periods beginning May 1, 2007 will be calculated as follows: Annual Total Value 
Added Charge net of the Reconciliation Charge divided by the number of therms the 
Company delivered to the customer during the Test Year: Beginning August 1, 2015 the 
Value Added Charge may be adjusted in accordance with Section F.4 this Service 
Classification.
Weighted Average Cost of Capacity 
(“WACOC”)
The unitized weighted average cost forecasted to be in effect for the upcoming month

unbundled Canadian pipeline transportation capacity used to deliver flowing gas 
supplies to the city gate, excluding transportation capacity used to deliver gas withdrawn 
from storage, plus 2) the fixed costs or basis premium of the Company’s bundled city 
gate winter supply contracts. The WACOC will be updated as required to reflect changes 
to rates and prices.

pipeline and storage provider rates.

Quick summary of changes for Definitions and Abbreviations section
1)
Definitions for all three companies listed in alphabetical order.
2)
Under Customer, all the other types of customers are now listed under 'Customer'.
3)
Under Applicants , all the other types of applicants are now listed under 'Applicants'.
4)
NMPC and KEDLI abbreviations now are all under 'Definitions' . KEDNY did not have abbreviations section. To be aligned with
NMPC and KEDLI, KEDNY will also shows similar abbreviations , but now in the Definitions section.
5)
Under NMPC, all definitions under Non Residential customers, are now in alphabetical order.
6)
For 'Dwelling & Applicants' - specific to certain jurisdictions, the Company is not changing definitions.
7)
For 'Applicants' and 'Customers', the Company is not proposing any changes to the definitions as these are specific to the
jurisdictions and the nature of the business.
8)
Incorporating 'Marketer' definition with 'Energy Service Company (ESCo)' definition since these are interchangeable.

RESUME OF HOWARD S. GORMAN 
SUMMARY 
Mr. Gorman has more than 30 years of experience in the energy industry, including 20 
years in rate and regulatory proceedings.  His areas of expertise include embedded class cost of 
service studies, marginal cost studies, revenue allocation, rate design and revenue requirements, 
for both electric and gas utilities.  He has testified as an expert witness before the Massachusetts 
Department of Public Utilities, New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, New Hampshire Public 
Utilities Commission, New York State Public Service Commission, Ontario Energy Board, 
Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission and Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.  Mr. 
Gorman also has experience in financial modeling, financial analysis and forecasting, developing 
accounting systems, and treasury and financial management. 
PROFESSIONAL EMPLOYMENT 
• 2010 - Present  
HSG Group, Inc. 
▪ President 
• 1997 - 2010 
 
Black & Veatch Corporation (R.J. Rudden Associates, Inc. before 
2005) 
▪ Principal Consultant 
• 1995 - 1997 
 
Independent Consultant 
• 1987 – 1995   
Trigen Energy Corporation 
▪ 1987-1993 Corporate Controller; Trigen was formed in 1987 
▪ 1993-1995 Treasurer; Trigen had IPO with NYSE listing in 1994 
• 1982 - 1987 
 
Coleco Industries, Inc. 
▪ Director, Treasury 
• 1976 - 1979 
 
Touche Ross & Co. 
▪ Staff Accountant 
PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE 
Utility Accounting and Costing 
Mr. Gorman has performed numerous class cost of service studies for electric and gas 
utilities, and has also developed and supported revenue requirements, revenue allocation proposals 
and rate designs.  These assignments included development of test year data, establishment of cost 
causality, selection of allocation bases, development of allocators, and analysis of customer 
impacts and policy considerations. 
Energy Project Analysis 
Mr. Gorman has performed financial analyses of energy-related assets, including electric 
and gas distribution companies, power plants and transmission operators.  These analyses included 
development of cash flows and financial statements based on both regulatory and accounting 


--- Page 489 ---
  
  
Exhibit___(G-RDP-15) 
Resumes of the Gas Rate Design Panel 
Page 2 of 4 
 
 
presentations, and included review of assumptions, analysis of data, modeling and forecasting, 
sensitivity testing and stress testing. 
Energy Project Financing 
Mr. Gorman has negotiated and completed transactions including construction and term 
loans, tax-exempt bonds, taxable bonds, subordinated debt and asset-backed (receivables and 
inventory) revolving credit facilities.  He has worked successfully with lenders and borrowers to 
source and structure transactions and was instrumental in negotiating loan documents and in 
designing power sale and supply procurement contracts to be financed. 
Accounting and Financial Management 
Mr. Gorman has extensive experience in financial accounting.  As controller of Trigen 
Energy Corporation, he founded and built the finance and accounting function; developed reports, 
procedures and management tools; and managed subsidiary controllers across North America, 
including an IPO with NYSE listing.  He managed the corporate insurance portfolios and the 
benefit plans for Trigen Energy Corporation and for Coleco Industries and has bought and sold 
interest rate and currency forward contracts for the purpose of managing risk. 
Modeling and Decision Support 
Mr. Gorman is an accomplished modeler with expertise in spreadsheet applications.  He 
has developed analytical tools for valuations, projections and simulations.  These models have 
been applied to financial analysis, cost allocations, rate design and pricing, forecasting revenue 
requirements, and tax and accounting matters.  Several of these models have contained interactive 
modules for automated scenario testing and sensitivity analysis. 
PUBLICATIONS AND PRESENTATIONS 
“What Wall Street Needs From FERC,” published in R. J. Rudden Financial, LLC’s Energy 
Capital Markets Report, September 2002 
“A Balanced Look at Balance Sheets,” published in R.J. Rudden Financial, LLC’s Energy 
Capital Markets Report, June 2002 
 “Assessment of Retail Choice Programs,” presented at the American Gas Association Rate and 
Strategic Issues Committee Conference, March 2002 
 “The Remarkable Story on Enron,” published in Scudder’s Annual End of Year Issue, December 
2001 
EDUCATION 
New York University, B.S., Accounting, 1976 
Harvard Business School, MBA, 1981

Kellie I. Smith 300 Erie Blvd West Syracuse, New York 13202  
Education  
Le Moyne College, Syracuse, New York Masters of Business Administration—December 2000  
State University College at Oswego, Oswego, New 
York BS Accounting—August 1994  
Professional Experience  
Director, NY Pricing, Jun 2019 – Present 
I am responsible for the oversight of the study, analysis, and design of delivery service rates, rate 
contracts, surcharge adjustment factors, riders and terms and condition of service for National 
Grid USA’s three New York State gas utilities, including KEDNY, KEDLI, and Niagara 
Mohawk Power Corporation, and for Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation’s electric utility. 
 
Manager, NY Gas Pricing, Dec 2015 – Jun 2019  
My responsibilities included the supervision of the study, analysis and design of retail gas 
delivery service rates and terms and conditions for gas service, including testifying and 
supporting such rates and tariffs before the NYPSC for National Grid USA’s three New York 
State gas utilities – KEDNY, KEDLI and Niagara Mohawk. The gas pricing department is also 
responsible for providing customer service and billing support, negotiated contract support, and 
guidance in the interpretation and application of retail gas delivery service tariffs.  
Senior/Lead Pricing Analyst, NY Electric Pricing-National Grid, Jan 2006 – Dec 2015  
My responsibilities as lead analyst included analytical support for electric standby service 
including cost and regulatory analysis, deferral accounting process design, rate design, and 
discovery responses.  I also had responsibility for the development of various surcharge factors 
including the monthly and annual reconciliations for the Company’s electric commodity 
reconciliations and merchant function charges.  I was also the regulatory lead for several new 
initiatives including the development of residential time of use rates and the implementation of 
the NYPA residential agricultural discount program.  
Senior Financial Analyst, Planning and Financial Analysis- National Grid Feb 2000 – Jan 2006  
My responsibilities as senior analyst included the preparation of margin reports monthly for 
internal management review, the evaluation of margin variances, the preparation of monthly 
revenue analysis and development of the annual budget for margin related items.

Melissa M. Barnes, 300 Erie Blvd West Syracuse, New York 13202  
Education  
Utica College of Syracuse University - Utica, New York 
BS Accounting/CPA – May 1996  
Professional Experience  
Manager, NY Gas Pricing, September 2019 - Present  
I am responsible for the supervision of the study, analysis and design of retail gas delivery service 
rates and terms and conditions for gas service, including testifying and supporting such rates and 
tariffs before the NYPSC for National Grid USA’s three New York State gas utilities – KEDNY, 
KEDLI and Niagara Mohawk. The gas pricing department is also responsible for providing 
customer service and billing support, negotiated contract support, and guidance in the 
interpretation and application of retail gas delivery service tariffs.  
Lead Analyst, NY Revenue Requirements - National Grid, Oct 2014 – Sept 2019  
My responsibilities as lead analyst included support for the various components of each 
Company’s (NMPC, KEDLI and KEDNY) cost of service and for the development of the revenue 
requirements included in various rate case proceedings.  In addition, I was also responsible for 
each Company’s annual excess earnings reports and various compliance filings filed with the 
Public Service Commission.  
Senior/Lead Pricing Analyst, NY Electric Pricing - National Grid, Feb 2008 – Oct 2014  
My responsibilities as lead analyst included the development of Niagara Mohawk’s electric retail 
revenue forecasts filed in various rate case proceedings, accounting support for various regulatory 
deferrals, rate design, and discovery responses.  I also had responsibility for the development of 
various surcharge factors including the monthly and annual reconciliations for the Company’s 
electric revenue decoupling mechanism and commodity reconciliation charges.  I was also the 
regulatory lead for the NYPA Replacement and Expansion Power petition filing along with the 
development and implementation of Niagara Mohawk’s revenue decoupling mechanism.  
Senior Analyst, Rhode Island Special Billing - National Grid May 2007 – Feb 2008  
My responsibilities as senior analyst included supporting the transition of the Rhode Island billing 
process to Syracuse, New York, preparation and review of customer bills, maintaining the billing 
system with the appropriate effective rates and customer contract terms and the development of 
internal controls within the special billing process.  
Senior Auditor, Internal Audit - National Grid Mar 2003 – May 2007  
My responsibilities as senior auditor included performance of various operational and financial 
internal audits, preparation of internal audit reports, communication of audit recommendations 
with various levels of management and tracking and closing of the audit recommendations.
